summary: Describes the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP), a reliable transport protocol that can carry multiple independent message streams in one connection. It was later replaced by RFC 4960.

plainLanguage.summary: SCTP is a transport protocol like TCP, but it carries whole messages instead of a stream of bytes, and it keeps several independent conversations apart so that a delay in one does not hold up the others. It can also use more than one network address at each end, so the connection keeps working if one path fails.

questions: how does the sctp four-way handshake work
how is sctp different from tcp
subtitle: A message-oriented transport protocol that carries several conversations at once and can survive a broken path.

tldr.problem: TCP forces strict ordering of all data, has no message boundaries, handles multi-homed hosts poorly and is vulnerable to SYN attacks, all of which hurt applications such as telephone signalling over IP.
tldr.mechanism: SCTP sets up an association with a four-way cookie handshake, carries user messages as chunks on independent streams, acknowledges data by TSN with selective acks, and can use several IP addresses at each end.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2960 is the original SCTP specification. It was obsoleted by RFC 4960 and updated by RFC 3309.

today: RFC 2960 is the original SCTP specification. It was obsoleted by RFC 4960 and updated by RFC 3309, so the current definition of SCTP is RFC 4960.

sections.title: Introduction: Why a Second Transport Protocol
sections.content:
TCP has performed immense service as the primary means of reliable data transfer in IP networks, but an increasing number of applications found it too limiting and built their own reliable transfer protocol on top of UDP. The limitations they wanted to bypass were that TCP provides both reliable transfer and strict order-of-transmission delivery, so applications that need reliable transfer without sequence maintenance or with partial ordering suffer from the head-of-line blocking TCP offers; that the stream-oriented nature of TCP is an inconvenience, because applications must add their own record marking to delineate messages and use the push facility to make sure a complete message is transferred in a reasonable time; that the limited scope of TCP sockets complicates highly available data transfer with multi-homed hosts; and that TCP is relatively vulnerable to denial of service attacks such as SYN attacks.

Transporting telephone signalling across the IP network is an application for which all of these limitations are relevant, and it directly motivated the development of SCTP, although other applications may find SCTP a good match to their requirements.

SCTP is a layer between the SCTP user application and a connectionless packet network service such as IP. Its basic service is the reliable transfer of user messages between peer SCTP users, performed within the context of an association between two SCTP endpoints. SCTP is connection-oriented, but the association is a broader concept than the TCP connection: during association startup each endpoint gives the other a list of transport addresses, meaning multiple IP addresses combined with an SCTP port, through which it can be reached and from which it will originate SCTP packets. The association spans transfers over all the possible combinations of those addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP is a single pipe: everything sent goes in one order, and a lost piece holds up everything behind it. SCTP was written for traffic such as telephone signalling, where messages must arrive reliably but do not all have to arrive in step, and where a machine may have several network addresses.

sections.title: What SCTP Adds: Streams, Messages and Paths
sections.content:
In SCTP a stream is a sequence of user messages that are delivered to the upper layer in order with respect to other messages in the same stream, which is not how the word is used in TCP, where it means a sequence of bytes. The SCTP user states at association startup how many streams the association will support, and that number is negotiated with the remote end. Messages are associated with stream numbers, and SCTP assigns a stream sequence number to each message. On the receiving side, SCTP ensures that messages are delivered in sequence within a given stream, while one stream may be blocked waiting for the next in-sequence message, delivery from other streams may proceed. A mechanism also allows messages to be delivered as soon as they are received, bypassing the sequenced delivery service.

When needed, SCTP fragments user messages so that the packet passed to the lower layer conforms to the path MTU, and reassembles the fragments into complete messages before handing them to the user. Each user data fragment or unfragmented message gets a Transmission Sequence Number, which is independent of the stream sequence number. The receiving end acknowledges all TSNs received even if there are gaps, which keeps reliable delivery separate from sequenced stream delivery.

An SCTP packet consists of a common header followed by one or more chunks, and the user may ask for several messages to be bundled into a single packet. The common header holds a mandatory Verification Tag, chosen by each end during startup, and a 32-bit checksum computed with Adler-32. Packets that arrive without the expected Verification Tag are discarded, which protects against blind masquerade attacks and against stale packets from an earlier association, and a packet with an invalid checksum is silently discarded.

Path management chooses the destination address for each outgoing packet from the addresses the user allows, using heartbeats when other traffic is not enough to tell whether a path is still working, and a primary path is defined for each endpoint at startup. An association is closed gracefully on request, or aborted when an error is detected; SCTP has no half-open state in which one side keeps sending while the other is closed.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ideas do most of the work. First, messages belong to separate streams, so a missing message in one stream does not hold up the others. Second, each end can list several addresses, and the protocol keeps an eye on which of them still work.

sections.title: The SCTP Packet: Common Header and Chunks
sections.content:
An SCTP packet is composed of a common header and chunks, and a chunk holds either control information or user data. Multiple chunks can be bundled into one packet up to the MTU size, except for the INIT, INIT ACK and SHUTDOWN COMPLETE chunks, which must not be bundled with any other chunk. If a user data message does not fit into one packet it is fragmented into multiple chunks. All integer fields are transmitted in network byte order.

The common header has four fields. The Source Port Number and Destination Port Number are 16 bits each; the receiver uses the destination port to hand the packet to the right endpoint or application, and the source port together with the addresses helps identify the association. The Verification Tag is 32 bits and validates the sender: on transmit it must be set to the value the peer supplied in its Initiate Tag, except that a packet carrying an INIT chunk must have a zero Verification Tag. The Checksum is 32 bits and uses the Adler-32 algorithm.

Each chunk is formatted with a Chunk Type field, a chunk-specific Flag field, a Chunk Length field and a Value field. The chunk type is 8 bits and takes a value from 0 to 254, with 255 reserved for future use as an extension field. The values define the chunk types: 0 is Payload Data, 1 Initiation, 2 Initiation Acknowledgement, 3 Selective Acknowledgement, 4 Heartbeat Request, 5 Heartbeat Acknowledgement, 6 Abort, 7 Shutdown, 8 Shutdown Acknowledgement, 9 Operation Error, 10 State Cookie, 11 Cookie Acknowledgement and 14 Shutdown Complete. The highest-order two bits of the chunk type say what an endpoint must do when it does not recognise the type: stop processing and discard the packet, and in some cases also report an unrecognised parameter.

The DATA chunk carries the user data. It holds the TSN (32 bits, wrapping back to zero after 4294967295), the Stream Identifier S (16 bits) and the Stream Sequence Number n (16 bits), a Payload Protocol Identifier (32 bits) supplied by the application, and the user data itself, padded with zero bytes to a 4-byte boundary but with the padding left out of the length field and never more than 3 bytes long. Three flags describe the message: the U bit marks the chunk as unordered, so no stream sequence number is assigned and the receiver must ignore that field; the B bit marks the first fragment of a message; and the E bit marks the last. Both B and E set means an unfragmented message, B alone the first piece, E alone the last piece, and neither set a middle piece. When a message is fragmented, the TSNs of its fragments must be strictly sequential.
sections.plainLanguage: Every SCTP packet starts with the same four fields: the two ports, a verification tag that proves the packet belongs to this association, and a checksum that catches damage in transit. The rest of the packet is a list of chunks, each one carrying either a piece of user data or a control instruction.

sections.title: Setting Up an Association: The Four-Way Handshake
sections.content:
The initialization has four steps. Endpoint A first sends an INIT chunk to endpoint Z, providing its Verification Tag in the Initiate Tag field, and then starts the T1-init timer and enters the COOKIE-WAIT state. Z replies immediately with an INIT ACK, setting the Verification Tag field to Tag_A and providing its own Tag_Z in the Initiate Tag field, and it must generate and send a State Cookie along with the INIT ACK. After sending the INIT ACK with the State Cookie parameter, Z must not allocate any resources or keep any state for the new association, because otherwise it would be vulnerable to resource attacks.

On receiving the INIT ACK, A stops the T1-init timer, sends the State Cookie back in a COOKIE ECHO chunk, starts the T1-cookie timer and enters the COOKIE-ECHOED state. The COOKIE ECHO chunk can be bundled with pending DATA chunks but must be the first chunk in the packet, and until the COOKIE ACK comes back the sender must not send any other packets to the peer. Z replies with a COOKIE ACK after building its transmission control block and moving to the ESTABLISHED state, and when A receives the COOKIE ACK it moves from COOKIE-ECHOED to ESTABLISHED and stops the T1-cookie timer. An INIT or INIT ACK chunk must not be bundled with any other chunk, and an endpoint must send the INIT ACK to the IP address from which it received the INIT.

The state cookie means the responder commits no state until the initiator has proved it received the cookie, so a flood of connection requests cannot exhaust its memory. The cookie mechanism is similar to one described by Karn and Simpson, and the last two legs of the handshake are allowed to carry user data for a fast setup. The association moves through the states CLOSED, COOKIE-WAIT, COOKIE-ECHOED and ESTABLISHED, and later through SHUTDOWN-PENDING, SHUTDOWN-SENT and SHUTDOWN-RECEIVED before returning to CLOSED. The stream counts are negotiated in the INIT and INIT ACK: each side states the number of outbound streams it wants and the maximum inbound streams it will accept, and if the peer's maximum inbound is smaller than the requested outbound count, the endpoint must either use the smaller number or abort the association and report the shortage to its upper layer.
sections.plainLanguage: Setting up takes four messages instead of three. The second message carries a cookie, a small piece of server state that the client sends straight back, so the server only commits memory once it knows the client is real. That is what makes floods of connection attempts cheap to refuse.

sections.title: Data Transfer, Multiple Addresses and Faults
sections.content:
An SCTP endpoint is multi-homed when more than one transport address can be used to reach it. The user picks one of the peer's addresses as the primary path, and by default the endpoint always transmits to the primary path unless the user asks for a specific destination. Reply chunks such as SACK and HEARTBEAT ACK should go back to the address the packet came from, and when the peer is multi-homed the sender should try to retransmit a chunk to an active destination address different from the last one it used. When the primary path becomes inactive, the sender may automatically switch to an alternate active address.

Faults are handled with two counters. An endpoint keeps a count of consecutive retransmissions to its peer, and when that count exceeds the parameter Association.Max.Retrans the peer is considered unreachable, the association moves to CLOSED and the failure is reported to the upper layer. The counter is reset whenever a DATA chunk is acknowledged or a HEARTBEAT ACK arrives. For a multi-homed peer, the endpoint keeps a separate error counter for each destination address, incremented when the T3-rtx timer expires on that address or a heartbeat to an idle address is not answered within a RTO; when the counter exceeds Path.Max.Retrans, that address is marked inactive and the upper layer is told. Heartbeats are sent periodically to idle addresses, and the suggested HB.interval is 30 seconds.

Congestion control in SCTP works on the association rather than on an individual stream, and an endpoint must not be more aggressive than the slow start and congestion avoidance algorithms allow. The three control variables are the receiver advertised window, the congestion window and the slow-start threshold. The biggest difference from TCP is multi-homing: a sender keeps a separate congestion control parameter set for each destination address, and it does slow start again on the first transmission to an address.
sections.plainLanguage: When a path fails, SCTP notices by the absence of acknowledgements, and it tries another address if the peer has one. Each address is tracked separately, so one bad path does not make the whole association look dead.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
SCTP is designed to reliably carry time-sensitive user messages, such as billing or signalling messages for telephony services, between two networked endpoints, and it has two security objectives: availability of reliable and timely data transport services, and integrity of the user-to-user information it carries. The memo expects operators to analyse their own risk situations and choose the countermeasures, and it points them at RFC 2196 for securing the site.

Against data corruption in the network, the memo says the IP Authentication Header should be used when the threat environment requires stronger integrity protection but not confidentiality, since protection applied only in the application layer would leave the SCTP header open to deliberate attacks. For confidentiality, the risk usually applies to the signalling payload rather than to the protocol overheads, so encrypting the SCTP user data alone may be enough, though ESP should be used instead where the requirement includes masking IP addresses and ports, as it does for mobile users. Whenever ESP is in use, an ESP transform that includes integrity protection must be used, because a confidentiality threat implies a strong integrity threat as well, and application-level encryption is then generally not required. Wherever confidentiality is provided, ISAKMP and the Internet Key Exchange should be used for key management.

Blind denial of service attacks take the form of flooding, masquerade and improper monopolization of services. Against flooding, protection begins at the equipment design level, with measures such as avoiding the commitment of limited resources before a request for service is known to be legitimate. The Verification Tag and the state cookie are the two mechanisms that protect against blind masquerade and against the memory exhaustion of a flood of connection attempts. The memo also notes that SCTP does not by itself protect against fraud and repudiation.
sections.plainLanguage: SCTP protects itself against two things: packets that pretend to belong to the association, and floods of connection attempts. For everything else, the memo points at IPsec, the security layer that already exists underneath it.

fields.desc: The port the packet is destined for.

fields.desc: Value the peer supplied during startup; packets without it are discarded.

messages.label: INIT
messages.note: Carries the initiator's tag and its stream and address lists.

messages.label: INIT ACK
messages.note: Carries the responder's tag and a state cookie. No state is kept yet.

messages.label: COOKIE ACK
messages.note: The responder now builds its state and moves to ESTABLISHED.
